Did you hear AI tools let engineers crank out 30% more code?  
But the review bottleneck grew by almost half, so nothing ships faster.  
Makes you wonder if the hype is missing the real cost.

Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton reveal a surprising twist: AI‑assisted coding agents boost raw code output by roughly 30 percent, yet the amount of finished, ship‑ready work stays flat.

The study, covering 718 firms and nearly 726 k engineers from January 2021 to March 2026, shows that while engineers wrote more lines, the average pull‑request review cycle lengthened by about 49 percent after AI adoption.

Additional signals reinforce the shift: AI‑generated pull requests now exceed 17 million per month, and legal‑AI tools keep a human reviewer in the loop, highlighting that the bottleneck has moved downstream.

“The faster drafting phase simply pushes the bottleneck to human review.”  

This matters because the hidden cost of slower reviews can erase the time saved in drafting, affecting overall delivery speed and ROI calculations for AI tools.

The analysis relies on Jellyfish engineering‑activity data and LinkedIn employment records, using a staggered difference‑in‑differences design to isolate the effect of AI adoption.

Given these findings, how should teams balance AI‑driven drafting gains with the need for reviewer capacity or automated gate‑keeping?
